title: Pauri 26, sound: amul gun

segments.voice: Yesterday, daat, the gift, even in hard things. Your line was even this is a gift. Did anything small that went wrong hide something? Today, Japji walks into a marketplace. Day two hundred five.

Picture an old bazaar in Punjab. Spice sellers calling out. Cloth merchants unrolling silk. A man with brass scales weighing lentils, a woman haggling over the price of mangoes. Everything has a price, and everybody's arguing about it. Guru Nanak knew this world well; tradition says he worked for a time as a storekeeper, weighing out grain. So when Pauri 26 begins, it borrows the language of the market: traders, trade, storehouses, scales. And then it breaks every price tag.
screen: `AN OLD PUNJAB BAZAAR.` → `EVERYTHING HAS A PRICE.` → `PAURI 26 BREAKS THE TAGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 26, in the original: amul gun amul vaapaar. Four words. Amul, a-MOOL: without price, priceless. Built like asankh, countless: a, not, plus mul, price. We'll open amul fully tomorrow. Gun, said with the u of put, not like the English word: virtues, qualities. The good things in a person, or in God. Vaapaar, vaa-PAAR: trade, business, dealing. The same word Punjabis still use for running a shop. So: priceless the virtues, priceless the trade. Then the stanza keeps going, in paraphrase: priceless the traders, priceless the storehouses. Priceless those who come to deal, priceless what they take away. And on it goes: priceless the scales, priceless the weights. Every piece of the market, one after another, is stamped amul. Hear the drumbeat of it. Amul gun, amul vaapaar: the same word striking at the start of each half, the way asankh did three weeks ago. Say it quickly and it sounds like a merchant calling out his wares; say it slowly and it sounds like a prayer. The point of borrowing the market isn't to despise it. Sikhs are known for honest work, kirat karni, and many are shopkeepers and traders. It's to say that when it comes to the virtues of the One, and the dealing between the soul and God, the scale has no numbers on it. Today, just the sound. Amul gun.
screen: `AMUL — WITHOUT PRICE.` · `GUN — VIRTUES, QUALITIES.` · `VAAPAAR — TRADE, DEALING.` · `EVERY PART OF THE MARKET.` · then, large: `AMUL GUN.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: amul gun, amul vaapaar. Once like a merchant calling out, brisk and clear. Then slowly, like a prayer. Then once more, as a whisper. Then sit, and let one good quality in someone you love come to mind: their patience, their humor, their kindness. Don't put a price on it. Just hold it. The bell holds the time.
Vaapaar, trade, dealing. It opens amul gun, amul vaapaar: priceless the virtues, priceless the trade, and every part of the market after them.
Your line: amul gun. Today, next time you pay for something, let the line play, and think of one good thing in your life that has no price. Day two hundred five.

howItsDone: Pauri 26 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs, for whom honest work, kirat karni, is one of the three pillars of daily life, hear its market words with special closeness.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about shopping.
what it means: the virtues of the One, and the dealing between the soul and God, can't be priced.
what a scholar hears: tradition places Guru Nanak as a storekeeper at Sultanpur Lodhi; the stanza stamps amul on traders, stores, scales and weights one after another.

notes: Guru Nanak's work at the Nawab's granary/store in Sultanpur Lodhi is from the janamsakhi tradition; stated as 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Pronunciation of gun (virtue): described as having the u of 'put'; confirm (it is not English 'gun'). The 'say' field uses GUN for simplicity.
Kirat karni named as one of three pillars (with naam japna and vand chhakna); confirm.
